html:
In May 1703 Peter the Great founded a fortress on marshy islands where the Neva River meets the Baltic Sea. Around it grew Saint Petersburg, which he made Russia's capital in 1712.

The land had just been taken from Sweden in the Great Northern War. Peter wanted a port on the Baltic and a city facing Europe, which a later writer called "a window on Europe". The first building was the Peter and Paul Fortress.

The site was terrible for a city: swampy, cold and prone to floods. Tens of thousands of forced labourers, peasants, soldiers and prisoners, drained the ground and built it, and many died. Nobles and merchants were ordered to move there and build houses in stone.

The city became the seat of the tsars for two centuries, laid out on European lines with canals and grand squares. It ended the age when Russia was a world apart, trading mainly through the White Sea and the Volga. It was renamed Petrograd in 1914 and Leningrad in 1924, and took back its old name in 1991.
sum: In May 1703 Peter the Great founded a fortress on marshy islands where the Neva River meets the Baltic Sea. Around it grew Saint Petersburg, which he made Russia's capital in 1712.
